findings.summary: C2 says xargs adds words the judge cannot see, but only covers words appended at the end. xargs's replace string (-I, -i, --replace, BSD -J) puts those words anywhere in the command, so the bypass this rule closes stays open. This is the brief's own violation: a word the judge cannot see stands where the deny rules look.
findings.evidence: Branch binary built from ee4adf63, vloop fence check --phase review: `echo push | xargs -I{} git {} origin` → allow; `echo push | xargs -I X git X origin` → allow; `echo push | xargs -i git {} origin` → allow. Each one runs `git push origin`. Under C2 as written, `{}` is not a brace expansion (the brief says so), X is literal, and only a trailing expanded word is appended, so `git {} origin *` and `git X origin *` match no rule and stay allowed. skipXargs (internal/fence/judge.go) does not list J among the letters that take an argument, so on macOS `xargs -J % git % origin` reaches the judge as the command `% git % origin`, which is allowed and runs git push origin.
findings.fix: In C2's xargs bullet: when xargs has -I/-i/--replace (or BSD -J), every word of the command holding the replace string is an expanded word. Alternatively refuse those options with a pinned message, e.g. `xargs -I cannot be judged`. Also make skipXargs's option table explicit for -J. Add a worked-example line: `review  echo push | xargs -I X git X origin   → deny: git X origin is denied by the review fence (Bash(git push:*)): a word the shell expands may be any text`, or the refusal message, whichever is chosen.

findings.section: Worked example (# C2: `bash $O 'git status'`) / C2 (words before the command name)
findings.summary: The line pins `$O expands before the command name and cannot be judged`, but the contract does not produce that answer for it. `$O` is not an option word before the -c string: shellString classifies it as a script name, and today's answer is `bash: runs a script or stdin, not a literal -c string`. Today it is already denied, so the line closes no hole. Errors reached through shellString also carry a `bash: ` prefix, and the pinned message lacks one.
findings.evidence: vloop fence check --phase review --tool bash "bash \$O 'git status'" on ee4adf63 → `deny: bash: runs a script or stdin, not a literal -c string`. Meanwhile `bash -$O -c 'git status'` → allow (the real gap). In judge.go the sh/bash case returns fmt.Sprintf("%s: %s", name, e) for shellString errors.
findings.fix: Replace the line with `review  bash -$O -c 'git status'   → deny: -$O expands before the command name and cannot be judged`. In C2, say whether that message carries the `bash: ` prefix (pin it either way). If the `bash $O` line stays, say that every word before the -c string is checked for expansion before shellString classifies it.

findings.section: Behaviour contract / C2 (Unchanged: a redirection target holding a glob is judged as written)
findings.summary: The brief keeps a word the shell expands matched as written for redirection targets, which is the very fault C2 fixes. In a work session that lets a write past the S-4 boundary at the hook. The brief cites S-4 for this run's own redirections but gives no reason for keeping the gap and does not name it out of scope.
findings.evidence: On ee4adf63, vloop fence check --phase work: `echo x > .gi?/config` → allow; `echo x > .vl?op/state/state.json` → allow. Bash expands a pathname in a redirection word when it yields one file, so these write .git/config and .vloop/state/state.json. docs/domain/domain-model.md:220 (S-4). The driver catches part of this afterwards (a changed .git/config entry or hook halts, and .vloop/ files are restored; fence-audit.md 'driver' bullet), but the hook does not.
findings.fix: Either refuse an unquoted glob or brace expansion in a redirection target, as `$` is refused today, with a pinned message such as `a redirection target holding a glob cannot be resolved: <word>` and a worked-example line. Or move it to Out of scope with the reason (the driver's after-session checks cover .git/config, hooks and .vloop/) and a later issue. Under the delegation either is the author's call.

findings.section: Why this shape — An expanded word is any text
findings.summary: The costs listed for C2 (git diff "$BASE", find "$d", git diff -- src/*.go) leave out the most common case for a work session: `rm` of a glob or a variable. `rm *.tmp` and `rm "$f"` become `rm <any text>`, which `Bash(rm -rf:*)` can match, so both are denied in work sessions, where rm of a file is allowed on purpose. The same goes for `git log -- *.go` and `git show $SHA`.
findings.evidence: fence/work.json index 21 `Bash(rm -rf:*)`. The work phase drops the rm:* stem (judge.go New), and fence-audit.md:225 says 'rm of a file is allowed in a work session: deleting and renaming files is part of the work'. Today `rm src/*.tmp` is allowed in a work session; under C2 the word stands for any text, including `-rf x`.
findings.fix: Add `rm "$f"` / `rm src/*.tmp` in a work session to the costs paragraph, so the operator approves it knowingly. A session writes the path out instead.

decisions: Drop the leading keyword and judge the rest, rather than parsing the grammar with mvdan.cc/sh. Sound: nothing is judged less than one command per line.
case, select, function, coproc, [[ and function definitions stay refused. Agreed. None appears in the counted denials.

An expanded word ($, glob, brace) is any text, and the whole word stands for it, not just the expanded part. Safe, but it over-denies: git diff "$BASE", find "$d", and, unlisted, rm "$f" in work sessions (finding 4).
Quoting makes $, globs and braces literal, and {…} without , or .. is not a brace expansion. Agreed. The splitter must start recording per-character quoting, which it drops today.
command -v / -V run nothing (only command, not time). Agreed.
Subshells are read, `((` is refused, and the other arithmetic contexts (let, ${a[x]}, declare -i) are left out of scope. Acceptable as scoped.
xargs input counts as a trailing expanded word. Right direction, but incomplete (finding 1).
A word a wrapper skips that is expanded refuses the command, and assignments before the name do not. Agreed.
A keyword after a wrapper is not dropped (`env ! x` stays denied). Agreed, conservative.
A redirection target holding a glob is judged as written. I would refuse it like `$` (finding 3).
Order inside a command: keywords, then closing/for/refused words, then assignments and wrappers. Agreed. It makes `X=1 if` stay denied.
